title: The Boat of the Body
summary: Saraha makes the body a sound little boat with the mind as its oar: the listener is told to hold the patabāla with the true guru's word, steady the mind, and let go and go by the innate, while a boatman hauls the boat by the towrope, fear waits on the road and the wave of existence sinks everything; keeping to the shore, it goes upstream in the strong current until, Saraha says, it is absorbed in the sky. Munidatta says the body is imagined as the boat and mental consciousness as the oar, takes the true guru's word as the patabāla, and reads the strong current as the stream of the passion of great bliss by which the bodhicitta-vajra rises and is absorbed in 'the island of the stainless wheel' (cp.38.m2, cp.38.m5).

lines.gloss: body · little boat · sound (genuine?) · mind · oar
lines.en: The [body]{body} is a sound little [boat]{boat}, the [mind]{citta} the [oar]{keruala}.

flags.note: khāṇṭi is uncertain. Chosen: 'sound', taking it as modern Bengali khā̃ṭi, 'genuine, pure, unadulterated'. Alternatives: 'genuine' or 'real' (the same word, more literally); or 'piece, plank', as the Tibetan line seems to read it (gru yi dum bu, 'a piece of a boat', as if from Sanskrit khaṇḍa). Munidatta cites the word (khaṇṭī) without explaining it (cp.38.m2). Compare khāṇṭabi in 4a.

ṇābaṛi is a diminutive of nāva, 'boat', hence 'little boat'. keṛuāla is the glossary's 'oar' (perhaps a steering paddle); Munidatta calls it kelipāta (cp.38.m2), and the Tibetan uses skya ba, 'oar', both here and for the patabāla of 1b.

lines.gloss: by/with the true guru's word · hold! · patabāla (a part of the boat) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: With the true [guru]{guru}'s word, hold the [patabāla]{patabala}.

flags.note: patabāla is kept in source form; its sense is uncertain. It may be the helm or a steering oar, since it is held (dhara): the Tibetan comment on couplet 3 renders Munidatta's karṇadhāra, 'helmsman', as skya ba 'dzin pa, 'oar-holder', the very phrase of the Tibetan line here (cp.38.m3). It may instead be the sail, if pata is paṭa, 'cloth'. Munidatta only repeats it as patavāla (cp.38.m2). The Tibetan line has skya ba, 'oar', its word for keṛuāla in 1a too.

sadgurubaaṇe ends in -e, which can be instrumental ('with, by the true guru's word') or locative ('in it'). Chosen: 'with', keeping the word as the means of holding. Munidatta sets 'the true guru's word' and 'the patavāla' side by side, as if the word were the thing held (cp.38.m2); the Tibetan line makes it a genitive, 'the oar of the true guru's speech'.

lines.gloss: mind · steady · having made · hold! (dhahu + re, 'O') · boatman (or: not; or: boat)

flags.note: nāhī has three possible senses. (1) Chosen: a boatman, addressed, since dhahure reads as dhahu, 'hold', plus the address particle re, 'O'; the Tibetan line ends gru pa rnams, 'boatmen' (plural). (2) The negative nāhī, 'no, not', running into 2b: '…and hold it. No: by any other means one cannot get across', an emphatic doubled negative with 2b's ṇa. (3) 'Boat' (compare nāī, 'boat', in other songs): 'hold the boat'. Munidatta's paraphrase here, 'protect the body-boat, O Sarahapāda' (cp.38.m2), has both a boat and an address, so it does not decide between (1) and (3).

The object of 'hold' is not expressed; 'it' is supplied, taking the steadied mind as the object, as the Tibetan does (sems nyid brtan pa nyid du bzung, 'hold the mind itself in steadiness'). If nāhī means 'boat', the boat is the object instead.

lines.translit: ana upāye pāra ṇa jāi || dhru ||
lines.gloss: other · by means · across (far shore) · not · goes · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: By any other [means]{upaya} one cannot get [across]{para}.

lines.gloss: boatman · boat · hauls · by the towrope

flags.note: guṇe: 'towrope' (the glossary's guna-towrope), the rope by which a boat is hauled from the bank. Munidatta's simile has the boat 'drawn with the guṇa' (guṇenākarṣayati) (cp.38.m3), which suits a rope. The Tibetan reads guṇa as yon tan, 'quality', in the line and in its comment.

naubāhī: 'boatman', the glossary's rendering and the song's own word (nau, 'boat', and vāh-, 'drive, carry'). Munidatta cites the word as novāa, and his simile has the helmsman (karṇadhāra) driving and towing the boat (cp.38.m3); the draft does not import 'helmsman' into the line.
The Tibetan line, gru ni 'bab pa gru shing mnyen pa'i yon tan yin, has the boat flowing down ('bab pa) and 'the quality (yon tan)' of the boat's mnyen pa: no boatman, no towing and no rope.

lines.translit: meli mela sahajem̐ jāu ṇa āṇem̐ || dhru ||
lines.gloss: having let go · let go! · by the innate · go · not · by another · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: Letting go, let go: go by the [innate]{sahaja}, not by another.

flags.note: meli mela. Chosen: two forms of the verb mel-, 'let go, release' (compare Bengali and Assamese mel-, 'open, spread, let loose'): meli, 'having let go', and mela, 'let go!'. The Tibetan line reads mela as a noun, 'gathering' (tshogs zhing tshogs pas, 'by gathering upon gathering'). A third possibility is mil-, 'join', with mela, 'union', as in song 27. Munidatta does not cite the words, but at this point he tells the yogin to give up the boat (cp.38.m3), which suits 'let go'.
jāu may be 'go!' or 'let it go' (the boat?); ṇa āṇem̐ is 'not by another' (āṇa, Sanskrit anya). The Tibetan has gzhan du shes, 'knows otherwise', perhaps from a reading like jāṇa, 'knows'.

lines.gloss: on the road · fear · will block (?) · the strong
lines.en: On the [road]{road} there is [fear]{bhaya}: the strong will block you.

flags.note: khāṇṭabi is a future form of a verb of unclear sense. Chosen: 'block', after the Tibetan line, which has 'the fear of obstruction' ('gog pa'i 'jigs pa). It may instead come from Sanskrit khaṇḍ-, 'break'. Munidatta cites khaṇṭa and explains it only as 'then the moon and the sun both become strong' (cp.38.m4).

balaā is taken as 'the strong', the subject, after Munidatta's balavantau, 'the two strong ones' (cp.38.m4). The verb has no expressed object; 'you', the listener addressed in couplets 1–3, is supplied. If -bi is a second-person future ending, the line could be 'you will block (or break) the strong'.

lines.translit: bhaba ulolem̐ ṣaa bi boliā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: existence · by the wave (surge) · all · even · sunk · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: By the [wave]{wave} of [existence]{bhava} everything is sunk.

flags.note: boliā: chosen 'sunk, drowned', after Munidatta's volita (cp.38.m4). The Tibetan line has 'became turbulent' (rnam par 'khrugs par gyur) and its comment 'became confused' ('khrul par gyur). ṣaa bi is 'all, even' (ṣ written for s), so 'everything'; the Tibetan makes 'all' qualify the waves.

lines.gloss: shore · having taken · in the strong · in the current · goes upstream
lines.en: Keeping to the [shore]{kula-shore}, it goes upstream in the strong [current]{current}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line, pha rol tshu rol chu rgyun drag po rab tu 'bab, has the strong current flowing down ('bab), where ujāa is 'goes upstream' (compare Bengali ujān, 'upstream'), and reads kula as 'far shore and near shore'. Munidatta has the bodhicitta-vajra 'go upward' (ūrdhvaṃ gacchati), and so does the Tibetan version of his comment (steng du 'gro) (cp.38.m5). The draft keeps 'upstream'.

kula lai, literally 'having taken the shore': chosen 'keeping to the shore', as a boat going upstream keeps near the bank; it could also mean 'reaching the shore'. The subject of ujāa is not expressed; 'it' (the boat, apparently) is supplied.

lines.gloss: Saraha · says · in the sky · is absorbed (?)
lines.en: [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: it is absorbed in the [sky]{gagana}.

flags.note: pamāem̐ is uncertain. Chosen: 'is absorbed', after Munidatta, who glosses 'in the sky' and goes on 'it is absorbed (antarbhavati) in the island of the stainless wheel' (cp.38.m5). The Tibetan line has nam mkha'i ting nge 'dzin, 'the concentration (samādhi) of the sky', as if reading samāem̐ or samāhi, 'in absorption'. Other derivations, such as pramāṇa, 'measure', are possible.
gaṇem̐ is taken as 'in the sky' (gaaṇa, Sanskrit gagana), as Munidatta (gagane, cp.38.m5) and the Tibetan (nam mkha') take it. The obvious alternative is gaṇ-, 'count': 'by reckoning'.

notes.text: Munidatta introduces the song by saying that Sarahapāda, full of loving-kindness (maitrīmaya), sets out the same meaning as before 'under the guise of the body-boat' (kāyanaukāvyājena) (cp.38.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has instead that he spoke it 'in twilight language, as a song on the body' (lus la glu dgongs pa'i skad kyis), with no boat.
Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung; this one by Bhairavī, which is also a name of a goddess.

The manuscript writes the attribution sarahapādānāṃ, 'of Sarahapāda', before the song; this edition removes it from line 1a, and the heading as given names only the rāga. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song b+hai ra bi zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs sa ra ha'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the song in the melody called Bhairavī, of Saraha', transcribing the rāga name; for song 12 it renders the same rāga as rnga bo che, 'great drum'.

Shastri prints ধ্রু, the cue to sing the refrain again, after couplet 1 as well as after couplets 2–4, and not after couplet 5. The refrain is couplet 2, which Munidatta comments on together with couplet 1 (cp.38.m2); he then counts couplet 3 as his second verse.

The image is a small river boat. The line itself makes the body the boat and the mind its oar; the patabāla of 1b is another part of the same boat, held in the hand; in 3a a boatman hauls the boat from the bank by a rope.

ṇābaṛi is a diminutive of nāva, 'boat', hence 'little boat'; Munidatta cites it as nāvaṛī (cp.38.m2). khāṇṭi is uncertain: the draft takes it as modern Bengali khā̃ṭi, 'genuine, pure', hence 'sound'. The Tibetan line, lus ni gru yi dum bu yid ni skya ba ste, 'the body is a piece (dum bu) of a boat, the mind is the oar', seems to read it as Sanskrit khaṇḍa, 'piece'. Munidatta cites the word (khaṇṭī) without explaining it. Compare khāṇṭabi in 4a.

patabāla: a part of the boat, which the listener is told to hold with the true guru's word; the source form is kept because its sense is uncertain. Because it is held (dhara), it may be the helm or a steering oar: the Tibetan version of Munidatta's comment on couplet 3 renders karṇadhāra, 'helmsman', as skya ba 'dzin pa, 'oar-holder', the very phrase of the Tibetan line here (skya ba 'dzin pa'o) (cp.38.m3). It may instead be the sail, if pata is paṭa, 'cloth'. Munidatta repeats it as patavāla without explaining it (cp.38.m2). The Tibetan line has skya ba, 'oar', its word for keṛuāla in 1a as well; the Tibetan comment has mnyen pa.

Munidatta says the body is imagined as the boat through the relation of support and supported (ādhārādheyasambandha), and mental consciousness (manovijñāna) as the oar, which he calls kelipāta. Where the song tells the listener to hold the patabāla with the true guru's word, his paraphrase has 'having taken the true guru's word, the patavāla', the two side by side (cp.38.m2).

Munidatta's comment on couplet 1 runs on into the refrain without a break. What he has made steady is not the mind of the song but conventional bodhicitta, 'having the nature of the five wisdoms, purified by vilakṣaṇa', in the middle of the ocean of existence that comes of the union of vajra and lotus; he then says 'protect the body-boat, O Sarahapāda', and, for 2b, that no other means exists for crossing the ocean of existence (cp.38.m2). He closes with a verse of Iuṛīpāda: 'these five go to the far shore of the river of delusion…' (ete pañca yaṃti mohataṭinīpāram). The song itself has a mind made steady and a crossing, with no ocean.

nāhī has three possible senses. (1) A boatman, addressed: dhahure is read as dhahu, 'hold', with the address particle re, 'O', so that nāhī is the one addressed; the Tibetan line ends with gru pa rnams, 'boatmen' (plural). The draft follows this. (2) The negative nāhī, 'no, not', running into 2b: 'hold it. No: by any other means one cannot get across', an emphatic doubled negative with 2b's ṇa. (3) 'Boat' (compare nāī, 'boat', in other songs): 'hold the boat'. Munidatta's paraphrase has at this point 'protect the body-boat, O Sarahapāda' (kāyanaurakṣāṃ kuru bho sarahapāda), which contains both a boat and an address, so it does not decide between (1) and (3) (cp.38.m2). If (1) stands, nāhī is a different word from naubāhī in 3a, though both are rendered 'boatman'.

For the refrain the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems nyid brtan pa nyid du bzung gis gru pa rnams / thabs gzhan gyis ni pha rol 'gro ba med, 'Hold the mind itself in steadiness, boatmen; by another means there is no going to the far shore.'
Towing: a boat is hauled with a rope by someone walking along the bank, usually against the current. This is what the boatman of 3a does.

The Tibetan line has gru ni 'bab pa gru shing mnyen pa'i yon tan yin, roughly 'the boat flows down: that is the quality (yon tan) of the boat's mnyen pa'. It seems to take naubāhī as the boat moving ('bab pa, 'flows down, descends') and guṇe as yon tan, 'quality'; it has no boatman, no towing and no rope. The Tibetan uses mnyen pa elsewhere for an oar or a helm.

Munidatta calls couplet 3 his second verse and says it states the praise (anuśaṃsā) of the path. Citing the line as novāa, he gives a simile: as outwardly the helmsman (karṇadhāra) drives the boat and draws it with the rope (guṇenākarṣayati), 'this boat is not like that' (tadvad iyaṃ naur na bhavati). He then tells the yogin to take the means of innate joy in the vajra guru and give up the boat (nauparityāgaṃ kuru), so as to go at once to the island of great bliss (cp.38.m3). The song shows the boatman hauling the boat; the Sanskrit comment sets this boat apart from that one and has it abandoned. The draft translates the song as it stands.

The Tibetan version of Munidatta's comment on couplet 3 differs at two points: 'likewise here the boat too is to be experienced' (de bzhin du 'dir gru ni yang nyams su myong ba'o), where the Sanskrit says this boat is not like the outer one; and 'do not abandon the boat' (gru ni yongs su ma spong cig), where the Sanskrit says to give it up. Its simile has the boat drawn 'by the quality (yon tan) of the oar-holder' (skya ba 'dzin pa'i yon tan gyis 'dren par byed), reading guṇa as 'quality' (cp.38.m3).

meli mela is taken here as two forms of the verb mel-, 'let go, release' (compare Bengali and Assamese mel-, 'open, spread, let loose'): meli, 'having let go', and mela, 'let go!'. The Tibetan line reads mela as a noun, 'gathering': tshogs zhing tshogs pas lhan cig skyes pas gzhan du shes, roughly 'by gathering upon gathering, through the innate, it is known otherwise'. A third possibility is mil-, 'join, meet', with mela, 'union', as in song 27 (melem̐). Munidatta does not cite the words, but at this point he tells the yogin to give up the boat (cp.38.m3), which suits 'let go'. jāu may be 'go!' or 'let it go'; āṇem̐ is 'by another' (Sanskrit anya). The Tibetan gzhan du shes, 'knows otherwise', may reflect a reading like jāṇa, 'knows'.

Munidatta says couplet 4, his third verse, states where the work of Māra takes hold (mārakarmādhiṣṭhāna). When the practitioner, through attachment to food, drink and sense objects, falls from the path, he abandons the avadhūtī (the clause avadhūtīṃ gatvā jahātīti is unclear). He explains khaṇṭa as 'then the moon and the sun both become strong' (balavantau), and says that for that reason, through the surging (ullālana) of the objects of the ocean of existence, the dharma of selflessness is volita, apparently 'sunk', in every way (cp.38.m4). The Tibetan version of the comment has 'became confused' ('khrul par gyur pa) for the last word.

khāṇṭabi is a future form of a verb khāṇṭ- whose sense is unclear. The draft follows the Tibetan line, lam ni 'gog pa'i 'jigs pa rnam par 'ong bar gyur, 'on the road the fear of obstruction ('gog pa) came', and has 'block'; it might instead come from Sanskrit khaṇḍ-, 'break'. balaā is taken as 'the strong', after Munidatta's 'the two become strong' (balavantau), the moon and the sun (cp.38.m4). The verb has no expressed object; 'you', the listener addressed in couplets 1–3, is supplied. If -bi is a second-person future ending, the line could be 'you will block (or break) the strong'.

ṣaa is saa, 'all' (the manuscript often writes ṣ for s), and bi is 'even, also': together, 'everything'. boliā is taken as 'sunk, drowned', after Munidatta's volita (cp.38.m4). The Tibetan line, srid pa'i dba' rlabs thams cad rnam par 'khrugs par gyur, 'all the waves of existence became turbulent', makes 'all' qualify the waves and the verb 'stirred up'. Munidatta paraphrases ulolem̐ as 'surging' (ullālana) and has 'the ocean of existence' where the song has existence. The glossary's 'play' (līlā) is detected inside ulolem̐ but is not in the line.

Munidatta calls couplet 5 his fourth verse, praising the path of the avadhūtī. He explains kula as the naturally purified avadhūtī 'in which the bad path (kumārga), the moon and the rest, goes to dissolution (laya)', apparently dividing the word as ku + la; lai (which he cites as laa) as 'having taken her'; the strong current as 'the whirl of the stream of the passion of great bliss', by which the bodhicitta-vajra of those who know the ultimate goes upward; and 'in the sky' as being absorbed 'in the island of the stainless wheel' (vaimalyacakradvīpa) (cp.38.m5). He does not say what the stainless wheel is.
A boat going upstream keeps close to the bank, where the current is slower and from where it can be towed; 'taking the shore' (kula lai) may describe this, or simply reaching the shore.

The Tibetan line has pha rol tshu rol chu rgyun drag po rab tu 'bab, 'far shore and near shore, the strong current flows mightily down'. It reads kula as both banks and has the current flow down ('bab), where the Bengali ujāa is 'goes upstream' (compare Bengali ujān, 'upstream'). The Tibetan version of Munidatta's comment, like his Sanskrit, has the bodhicitta-vajra 'go upward' (steng du 'gro bar byed) (cp.38.m5), so the Tibetan line disagrees with its own comment. The draft keeps 'upstream'.

pamāem̐ is uncertain. The draft has 'is absorbed', following Munidatta, who glosses 'in the sky' and goes on 'it is absorbed (antarbhavati) in the island of the stainless wheel' (cp.38.m5). The Tibetan line has sa ra ha yi zhabs kyis smras pa nam mkha'i ting nge 'dzin, 'Saraha said: the concentration (samādhi) of the sky', as if reading samāem̐ or samāhi, 'in absorption'. Other derivations, such as pramāṇa, 'measure', are possible. gaṇem̐ is taken as 'in the sky' (gaaṇa, Sanskrit gagana), as Munidatta and the Tibetan take it; gaṇ-, 'count', is the obvious alternative.

termsOmitted.reason: False hit: লোলেঁ is detected inside উলোলেঁ (ulolem̐, 'by the wave, surge'), which is rendered 'wave'. The line has no word for play (līlā); Munidatta paraphrases the word as ullālana, 'surging' (cp.38.m4).

questions: patabāla (1b): keep the source form, as drafted, or commit to 'helm' (it is held, and the Tibetan comment's skya ba 'dzin pa, 'oar-holder', for karṇadhāra echoes its line 1b) or to 'sail' (paṭa, 'cloth')? Munidatta only repeats the word.
guṇe (3a): keep the glossary's 'towrope', which Munidatta's simile of drawing the boat with the guṇa supports, though the Tibetan reads yon tan, 'quality', in both line and comment?
naubāhī (3a): keep 'boatman', the song's word, or follow Munidatta's simile, which has karṇadhāra, the glossary's 'helmsman'? The draft keeps 'boatman' in the line and puts the helmsman in the notes.

nāhī (2a): the draft has 'boatman', addressed, with the Tibetan gru pa rnams. Would you prefer the negative ('…hold it. No: by any other means…') or 'boat' ('hold the boat'), which Munidatta's 'protect the body-boat' might reflect? If 'boatman' stands, should নাহী be added as a form of the boatman entry, and should it be singular as drafted or plural as in the Tibetan?

meli mela (3b): the draft reads the verb 'let go' ('Letting go, let go'), which suits Munidatta's 'give up the boat' at this point. Accept this, or follow the Tibetan 'gathering' (tshogs), or read 'union' (mela) as in song 27?

ujāa (5a): the draft keeps 'goes upstream', against the Tibetan line's current that 'flows down' ('bab), since Munidatta and the Tibetan comment both have the bodhicitta-vajra go upward. Agreed? And is 'it' (the boat, apparently) acceptable as the supplied subject?

gaṇem̐ pamāem̐ (5b): the draft has 'it is absorbed in the sky', with gaṇem̐ as 'sky' and pamāem̐ after Munidatta's antarbhavati. The Tibetan has nam mkha'i ting nge 'dzin, 'the concentration of the sky'. Should the line keep 'absorbed', which can carry both senses, or be made more literal once pamāem̐ is settled?

khāṇṭabi balaā (4a): 'the strong will block you' rests on the Tibetan 'gog pa, 'obstruction', and Munidatta's balavantau, with 'you' supplied. Is the supplied object acceptable, or would you rather leave the line without one?
khāṇṭi (1a): the draft has 'sound' (Bengali khā̃ṭi, 'genuine'); the Tibetan dum bu suggests 'piece'. Is 'sound' acceptable?

Heading: the source heading names only the rāga, and the manuscript's attribution sarahapādānāṃ was removed from 1a. Should the English heading add '· Sarahapāda', as in the usual form 'Rāga X · Poet'?

Couplet 3: Munidatta's Sanskrit says 'this boat is not like that' and 'give up the boat', while the Tibetan version of his comment says 'likewise here the boat too is to be experienced' and 'do not abandon the boat'. How should the woven commentary present this: Sanskrit only, with the Tibetan in a witness note, as drafted?
